narrative:
The model predicted an 84.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is far below the average of roughly 6 among students who were accepted. Your first-year ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; again, a bottom-decile performance contrasts sharply with the typical accepted student who ranks around the 6th decile.

Your undergraduate GPA was the only one of these three factors that worked in your favor. At 3.60 it is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students, which helped reduce the predicted risk somewhat. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the impact of your low class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 27 (versus an accepted-student average of 37) and middle family income also contributed to the overall picture, though less strongly.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance in law school so that your class rank improves significantly. Retaking the LSAT and aiming for a much higher score would also help demonstrate stronger readiness. Consider reapplying once you have stronger evidence of your ability to excel in a legal academic environment. (248 words)
